{{short description|British biologist (1921–1999)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=February 2021}}
'''Arthur James Cain''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (25 July 1921 – 20 August 1999)<ref name= "Clarke2008">{{Cite journal |last1=Clarke |first1=B.C. | doi=10.1098/rsbm.2007.0034  | doi-access=free|title=Arthur James Cain. 25 July 1921 – 20 August 1999 |journal=[[Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society]] |volume=54 | pages=47–57 |year=2008 |s2cid = 73131707 }}</ref> was a British [[evolutionary biologist]] and [[ecologist]].  He was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 1989.

== Career ==
Arthur James Cain was born and grew up in [[Rugby, Warwickshire|Rugby]] in Warwickshire, England. In 1939 he was awarded a prestigious scholarship ([[Demyship]]) to [[Magdalen College, Oxford]], where he graduated with [[British undergraduate degree classification#First-class honours|first class honors]] in Zoology in 1941. Entering the British army in December 1941, Cain was commissioned [[second lieutenant]] in the [[Royal Army Ordnance Corps]] (engineering) and was later transferred to the [[Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers]] (R.E.M.E.) on its formation. He was promoted to [[Captain (British Army and Royal Marines)|captain]] in 1942.

After leaving the military in November 1945, Cain returned to Oxford to pursue research in the Department of Zoology. He became a Departmental Demonstrator in October 1946, finishing his [[Doctor of Philosophy|D. Phil.]] in 1948. From January 1949 until 1964 Cain was employed as University Demonstrator in Animal Taxonomy. In addition he was appointed [[Curator]] of the Zoological Collections at the [[Oxford University Museum]] in 1954, besides serving as Lecturer in Zoology at [[St Peter's College, Oxford|St Peter's College]] (1958–1961).

In 1964, Cain left Oxford to become professor of zoology at the [[University of Manchester]], and he later (1968) was appointed Derby Professor of Zoology at the [[University of Liverpool]]. He received [[emeritus]] status at Liverpool upon his retirement in 1989.<ref name="Clarke2008"/><ref name="APS">{{cite web |title=Arthur J. Cain Papers Mss.Ms.Coll.63 |url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/collections/view?docId=ead/Mss.Ms.Coll.63-ead.xml |publisher=American Philosophical Society |access-date=2 July 2024}}</ref><ref name="Cook2000">{{cite journal |last1=Cook |first1=L. |title=A.J. Cain F.R.S. 1921-1929 |journal=Malacological Bulletin |date=2000 |volume=34 |url=http://malacsoc.org.uk/malacological_bulletin/BULL34/CAIN.HTM |access-date=2 July 2024}}</ref>

== Scientific activities ==
Cain's main interests lay in [[evolutionary biology]], [[ecological genetics]], [[systematics|animal taxonomy]] and [[speciation]].

Though he initially conducted research with [[John Baker (biologist)|John Baker]] on the [[histochemistry]] of [[lipids]], his main work lay in the field developed by [[E.B. Ford]], namely, [[ecological genetics]]. With [[Philip Sheppard (biologist)|P.M. Sheppard]], Cain studied the ecological genetics of colour and banding [[polymorphism (biology)|polymorphisms]] in [[snails]]. Cain and Sheppard's work on ''[[Cepaea nemoralis]]'', one of the first studies to demonstrate natural selection by predators acting on a colour polymorphism, is now regarded as a classic. It generated a long series of further studies by Cain, including the formal [[genetic analysis]] of the variation, the discovery of area effects and the analysis of climatic influences. With [[John Donald Currey|John Currey]] he made elegant use of [[sub-fossil]] material to follow changes in time as well as space. Later he turned to the study of variation in shell shape.<ref name="Cook2024">{{cite journal |last1=Cook |first1=L.M. |title=Arthur Cain and ecological genetics in the Oxford Zoology Department |journal=Archives of Natural History |date=2024 |volume=51 |issue=1 |pages=73–85 |doi=10.3366/anh.20240897}}</ref>

In population genetics he clarified the concept of [[adaptive value]]. He made important contributions to the theory and practice of [[Taxonomy (biology)|taxonomy]], the problems of [[homology (biology)|homology]], [[cladism|phyletic weighting]] and taxonomic importance, on the status of the [[genus]], and on the relevance of [[natural selection]] to our understanding of variation between taxonomic categories.

== Cain reminisces on pre-war Oxford ==
Towards the end of his life Cain was persuaded to reminisce about the status of [[natural selection]] in pre-war Oxford and how it changed over the years of the [[modern synthesis (20th century)|modern evolutionary synthesis]].<ref>Cain A.J. and Provine W.B. 1991. Genes and ecology in history. In Berry R.J. & others (eds) ''Genes in ecology'': the 33rd Symposium of the British Ecological Society. Blackwell, Oxford.</ref><ref>Huxley J. 1942. ''[[Evolution: The Modern Synthesis|Evolution: the modern synthesis]]'' (2nd ed 1963, 3rd ed 1974)</ref> The general attitude was sceptical of natural selection. [[Charles Sutherland Elton|Charles Elton]], who led the emergence of [[ecology]] as a discipline, pointed out the [[Arctic fox]] polymorphism, which can be found in all three [[tundra]] [[biomes]] of the northern [[palaeoarctic]]. Arctic foxes (''[[Alopex lagopus]]'') are dimorphic: the common morph ('white') is white in winter and brownish-grey dorsally in summer; the other morph ('blue') is light brown/blue in winter and dark brown in summer. The two morphs interbreed freely. Despite the obvious advantage of white in avoiding predation, blue is actually the most frequent morph in [[Iceland]]. Elton also gave a number of other examples which he claimed could not be explained by natural selection.<ref>Elton C.S. 1927. ''Animal ecology''.</ref>

:''That very phenomenon which was to be used by Fisher & Ford in studies on natural selection is here shown by cogent argument and the facts of field natural history to be [apparently] inexplicable by selection. But Elton knew that a far greater range of other characters have the same implications, namely, all, or nearly all, the differences (non-polymorphic) between closely related species''. Cain.<ref>Cain & Provine W.B. 1991. Genes and ecology in history. In Berry R.J. ''Genes in ecology'' p5</ref>

Also, Robson and Richards<ref>Robson G.C. and Richards O.W. 1936. ''The variation of animals in nature''. Longmans, London.</ref> "showed a surprising reluctance to allow any example of natural selection; their cautious qualification that characters were non-adaptive as far as they could see became, too often, a certainty that they were non-adaptive; and their arguments were sometimes one-sided." Cain laid the blame on their "vitalistic or perhaps theistic attitudes... Robson and Richards were far from alone. [[Alister Hardy]]... was an earnest [[Unitarianism|Unitarian]] and certainly a [[vitalist]]" (p7)... In Cambridge matters were even worse" (p8, giving as examples [[William Homan Thorpe|W.H. Thorpe]], [[Charles E. Raven|Charles Raven]], Sir [[James Gray (zoologist)|James Gray]] and [[J.W.S. Pringle]]).

:''What I wanted to know from all these great people was, how exactly did they know that a character was non-adaptive or neutral? They didn't know, and they couldn't know.'' Cain.<ref>Cain & Provine W.B. 1991. Genes and ecology in history. In Berry R.J. ''Genes in ecology'' p8</ref> This was the stimulus for Cain's research on evolution in natural communities.

:''David Lack was the only religious man I knew at that period who did not allow his religion to dictate his view of natural selection.'' Cain.<ref>Cain & Provine W.B. 1991. Genes and ecology in history. In Berry R.J. ''Genes in ecology'' p9</ref>

He might have added, had he known them, [[Ronald Fisher]] and [[Theodosius Dobzhansky]], who were also believing Christians: Fisher from the start of his career was a leading proponent of natural selection.

In contrast to many others, [[E.B. Ford]] appreciated that, even if a character was in itself non-adaptive, the gene or genes determining it might affect other, adaptive, characters which were always under selective influence.<ref>Ford E.B. 1964, 4th edn 1975. ''Ecological genetics''. Chapman and Hall, London</ref><ref>Ford E.B. 1965. ''Genetic polymorphism''. All Souls Studies, Faber & Faber, London</ref> Ford understood the significance of [[pleiotropism]], and knew of [[Ronald Fisher|Fisher]]'s demonstration that a neutral gene derived from a single mutation could only be in about the same number of individuals as there had been generations since its inception.<ref>Fisher R.A. 1930. ''Genetical theory of natural selection'' p80.</ref> Also, as Cain's own research showed, much [[polymorphism (biology)|polymorphism]] is maintained by differential selection in the diversity of environments within a species' range.<ref>Cain A.J. and Currey J.D. 1963. Area effects in ''Cepaea''. ''Phil Trans Roy Soc B'' '''246''', 269–299.</ref><ref>Cain A.J. and Currey J.D. 1968. Ecogenetics of a population of ''Cepaea nemoralis'' subject to strong area effects. ''Phil Trans Roy Soc B'' '''253''', 447–482.</ref><ref>Clarke B.C. 1979. The evolution of genetic diversity. ''Proc Roy Soc B''. '''205''', 453–474.</ref>
